passages: Bitwise Asset Management has raised its Bitcoin price target to $1.6 million by 2036, up from its previous forecast of $1.3 million by 2035, citing expanding institutional demand and growing interest in assets that protect against currency debasement.

In its latest long term capital market assumptions report , the asset manager projected a compound annual growth rate of 34.3% for Bitcoin over the next decade, compared with the 28.3% annualized return estimated in last year's report.
The revised forecast comes despite Bitcoin losing 53% of its value between its October 2025 peak above $125,000 and its June 2026 low below $59,000.
Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan said he initially expected the market downturn and deteriorating macroeconomic conditions to force the firm to lower its long term outlook.
Instead, the updated model produced a higher valuation, driven primarily by increases in the size of markets that Bitcoin could potentially capture.
"Using the exact same model as last year with updated data, we're raising our 10-year forecast from $1.3 million to $1.6 million," Hougan wrote.

The asset manager maintained its previous assumptions about Bitcoin's share of each addressable market, meaning the higher target reflects larger market opportunities rather than more aggressive adoption estimates.
Bitwise's updated valuation model projects that the global store of value market will reach approximately $110 trillion over the next decade, up from its previous estimate of $91 trillion.
The firm also increased its projected institutional investment market from $216 trillion to $303 trillion, reflecting expectations of expanding financial assets and growing institutional demand.
According to Hougan, Bitcoin's potential valuation depends on two factors: the total size of the markets it can serve and the share of those markets it ultimately captures.
The report identifies store of value assets, institutional investment portfolios, offshore wealth and emerging market currencies among Bitcoin's potential opportunities.
Bitwise expects persistent inflation, rising government debt and currency debasement concerns to increase demand for scarce assets over the coming decade.
The firm argues that Bitcoin could benefit from these trends as investors seek alternatives to traditional fiat currencies and government debt.
Hougan also pointed to growing institutional adoption, including increased access through wealth management platforms such as Wells Fargo and Merrill Lynch.
He said central banks and sovereign wealth funds have also moved closer to digital asset exposure, while Bitcoin's historical volatility has gradually declined.
Despite these developments, Bitwise kept its market penetration assumptions unchanged from last year's model.
The firm estimates that Bitcoin's share of the broader store of value market has already increased from less than 1% a decade ago to more than 5%.
The report acknowledges that Bitcoin's recent performance has challenged investor confidence, particularly after its decline from record highs.
However, Bitwise argues that the 53% peak to trough loss was considerably smaller than the drawdowns exceeding 80% recorded during previous major Bitcoin bear markets.
The company interprets the smaller decline as a possible indication of a maturing market supported by a broader institutional investor base.
Hougan also noted that institutional investors continued adding Bitcoin exposure during the downturn, even as exchange traded fund inflows slowed.

The report highlights Bitcoin's increasing correlation with gold, although most of the recent demand for traditional store of value assets has flowed into the precious metal rather than cryptocurrencies.
Bitwise expects Bitcoin to remain volatile over the coming decade but projects that its price fluctuations will gradually moderate as institutional participation expands.
The firm also expects Bitcoin's traditional four year market cycle to become less influential as its investor base grows.

Still, the report cautions that significant drawdowns remain possible and identifies regulatory uncertainty, technological disruption and advances in quantum computing as potential risks to its assumptions.
Hougan said Bitcoin's ability to maintain institutional interest through a difficult market environment has strengthened his confidence in its longer term prospects.
The firm's outlook rests on continued institutional adoption, demand for hard assets and Bitcoin's limited supply.
Unlike conventional currencies, Bitcoin has a predetermined issuance schedule and a maximum supply of approximately 21 million coins.
Bitwise argues that this supply structure could become increasingly important if demand expands among institutional investors and other large capital allocators.
The asset manager expects Bitcoin to outperform major traditional asset classes over the next decade, although its forecast remains dependent on assumptions about market growth and adoption.

The report also projects that Bitcoin will maintain relatively low to moderate correlations with stocks, bonds and other major asset categories, potentially supporting its role in diversified investment portfolios.
Bitwise emphasized that the $1.6 million valuation is a model based projection rather than a guaranteed price outcome.

Its institutional investment assumption is 1%, against a projected market of $303.5 trillion.
Using the rounded table inputs, the store-of-value component contributes $27.45 trillion of Bitcoin’s modeled value.

Its exact base-case target is $1,599,766, alongside bear and bull scenarios of $130,686 and $3,667,911.

The forecast horizon moves forward by one year, from 2035 to 2036.

Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan linked the revised forecast to regulatory progress, institutional adoption and demand for hard assets, including gold.

In the release, the firm forecasts annual returns of 6.7% for US equities and 10.8% for private equity, below its Bitcoin estimate.
With institutions accounting for more of the investor base, Bitwise expects the historic four-year cycle to weaken, while warning that substantial downturns will remain possible.
On its research page, Bitwise projects average volatility of 27.8% and an average correlation of 0.43 with US stocks over the next decade.
The firm identifies quantum computing, AI-driven mathematical advances and regulatory reversal as major risks to its investment case.

Its digital-gold assumptions ranged from 20% to 60% of an $18 trillion gold market, which the model held constant through 2030.

ARK’s underlying study separately explored an active-supply approach that discounted lost or long-held coins, assuming only 60% of projected supply remained active by 2030.
6, 2025 report subsequently described Cathie Wood’s revised bullish target of $1.2 million, down from $1.5 million.
Citing her CNBC interview, the report said stablecoins were taking part of the payments and savings role ARK had previously expected Bitcoin to serve in emerging markets.

ViaBTC’s Ko sees accumulation alongside complacent positioning Commenting on recent market conditions, Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC, described Bitcoin’s trading as volatile but relatively constructive in comments to the publication.
“I think market positioning remains somewhat complacent, and it looks like an accumulation period,” Ko said.
According to Ko, funding rates remained positive while open interest had partially recovered from its September lows.
He said Bitcoin had reclaimed its 50-week moving average and held above it for four to five weeks, a development he described as encouraging.
In the same assessment, Ko said Bitcoin briefly recovered toward $84,000 before slipping below $80,000.

extraction.body: Bitwise Asset Management has raised its Bitcoin price target to $1.6 million by 2036, up from its previous forecast of $1.3 million by 2035, citing expanding institutional demand and growing interest in assets that protect against currency debasement. In its latest long term capital market assumptions report , the asset manager projected a compound annual growth rate of 34.3% for Bitcoin over the next decade, compared with the 28.3% annualized return estimated in last year's report. The revised forecast comes despite Bitcoin losing 53% of its value between its October 2025 peak above $125,000 and its June 2026 low below $59,000. Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan said he initially expected the market downturn and deteriorating macroeconomic conditions to force the firm to lower its long term outlook. Instead, the updated model produced a higher valuation, driven primarily by increases in the size of markets that Bitcoin could potentially capture. "Using the exact same model as last year with updated data, we're raising our 10-year forecast from $1.3 million to $1.6 million," Hougan wrote. The asset manager maintained its previous assumptions about Bitcoin's share of each addressable market, meaning the higher target reflects larger market opportunities rather than more aggressive adoption estimates. Bitwise's updated valuation model projects that the global store of value market will reach approximately $110 trillion over the next decade, up from its previous estimate of $91 trillion. The firm also increased its projected institutional investment market from $216 trillion to $303 trillion, reflecting expectations of expanding financial assets and growing institutional demand. According to Hougan, Bitcoin's potential valuation depends on two factors: the total size of the markets it can serve and the share of those markets it ultimately captures. The report identifies store of value assets, institutional investment portfolios, offshore wealth and emerging market currencies among Bitcoin's potential opportunities. Bitwise expects persistent inflation, rising government debt and currency debasement concerns to increase demand for scarce assets over the coming decade. The firm argues that Bitcoin could benefit from these trends as investors seek alternatives to traditional fiat currencies and government debt. Hougan also pointed to growing institutional adoption, including increased access through wealth management platforms such as Wells Fargo and Merrill Lynch. He said central banks and sovereign wealth funds have also moved closer to digital asset exposure, while Bitcoin's historical volatility has gradually declined. Despite these developments, Bitwise kept its market penetration assumptions unchanged from last year's model. The firm estimates that Bitcoin's share of the broader store of value market has already increased from less than 1% a decade ago to more than 5%. The report acknowledges that Bitcoin's recent performance has challenged investor confidence, particularly after its decline from record highs. However, Bitwise argues that the 53% peak to trough loss was considerably smaller than the drawdowns exceeding 80% recorded during previous major Bitcoin bear markets. The company interprets the smaller decline as a possible indication of a maturing market supported by a broader institutional investor base. Hougan also noted that institutional investors continued adding Bitcoin exposure during the downturn, even as exchange traded fund inflows slowed. The report highlights Bitcoin's increasing correlation with gold, although most of the recent demand for traditional store of value assets has flowed into the precious metal rather than cryptocurrencies. Bitwise expects Bitcoin to remain volatile over the coming decade but projects that its price fluctuations will gradually moderate as institutional participation expands. The firm also expects Bitcoin's traditional four year market cycle to become less influential as its investor base grows. Still, the report cautions that significant drawdowns remain possible and identifies regulatory uncertainty, technological disruption and advances in quantum computing as potential risks to its assumptions. Hougan said Bitcoin's ability to maintain institutional interest through a difficult market environment has strengthened his confidence in its longer term prospects. The firm's outlook rests on continued institutional adoption, demand for hard assets and Bitcoin's limited supply. Unlike conventional currencies, Bitcoin has a predetermined issuance schedule and a maximum supply of approximately 21 million coins. Bitwise argues that this supply structure could become increasingly important if demand expands among institutional investors and other large capital allocators. The asset manager expects Bitcoin to outperform major traditional asset classes over the next decade, although its forecast remains dependent on assumptions about market growth and adoption. The report also projects that Bitcoin will maintain relatively low to moderate correlations with stocks, bonds and other major asset categories, potentially supporting its role in diversified investment portfolios. Bitwise expects allocations from that pool to generate the projected demand.

extraction.body: Bitwise has raised its long-term Bitcoin price forecast to $1.6 million by 2036, citing institutional demand, limited new supply, and growing demand for assets that can protect against currency debasement. Bitwise projects 34.3% annualized Bitcoin returns over its model’s 10-year period. The valuation assumes Bitcoin captures 25% of a projected gold-and-Bitcoin store-of-value market. ViaBTC’s Jeff Ko describes recent trading as an accumulation period, while flagging complacent positioning. Bitwise Asset Management released its 2027 Bitcoin Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions on Oct. 28, setting out a decade-long investment case that rests on Bitcoin gaining ground in several markets, led by its use as a store of value. Bitcoin’s $1.6 million forecast rests on a growing store-of-value market In its valuation framework, Bitwise projects the combined gold-and-Bitcoin store-of-value market will reach $109.8 trillion by 2036, with Bitcoin taking 25%. The model assigns smaller contributions to institutional portfolios, emerging-market currencies, offshore wealth, national reserves, US corporate treasuries, and remittances. Its institutional investment assumption is 1%, against a projected market of $303.5 trillion. Using the rounded table inputs, the store-of-value component contributes $27.45 trillion of Bitcoin’s modeled value. Dividing that amount by the model’s 21 million-coin denominator produces approximately $1.31 million per coin before the other categories are included. Its exact base-case target is $1,599,766, alongside bear and bull scenarios of $130,686 and $3,667,911. As crypto.news previously reported in August 2025, the firm’s earlier Bitcoin forecast put its base case at $1.3 million by 2035, with an annualized return of 28.3%. The earlier report outlined a $3 million bull case and an $88,000 bear case. The forecast horizon moves forward by one year, from 2035 to 2036. Institutional allocations underpin Bitwise’s demand estimates In its accompanying announcement, Bitwise said institutional investors could allocate 1% to 5% of their portfolios to Bitcoin over the coming decade. The firm estimated potential demand at $1.5 trillion to $7 trillion, compared with roughly $14 billion in new Bitcoin produced annually at its reference valuation. Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan linked the revised forecast to regulatory progress, institutional adoption and demand for hard assets, including gold. “We are more bullish on bitcoin today than we were last year,” Hougan said in the announcement. In the release, the firm forecasts annual returns of 6.7% for US equities and 10.8% for private equity, below its Bitcoin estimate. With institutions accounting for more of the investor base, Bitwise expects the historic four-year cycle to weaken, while warning that substantial downturns will remain possible. On its research page, Bitwise projects average volatility of 27.8% and an average correlation of 0.43 with US stocks over the next decade. The firm identifies quantum computing, AI-driven mathematical advances and regulatory reversal as major risks to its investment case. ARK’s earlier targets use different adoption and supply assumptions ARK Invest’s April 2025 Bitcoin valuation study set 2030 bear, base and bull cases of approximately $300,000, $710,000 and $1.5 million. The firm modeled institutional investment, digital gold and emerging-market demand as its main contributors, with national reserves, corporate treasuries and on-chain financial services providing smaller contributions. Within that framework, ARK assumed institutional penetration of 1%, 2.5% and 6.5% across its three scenarios. Its digital-gold assumptions ranged from 20% to 60% of an $18 trillion gold market, which the model held constant through 2030. Coverage in April 2025 of ARK’s experimental supply model outlined a potential $2.4 million target. ARK’s underlying study separately explored an active-supply approach that discounted lost or long-held coins, assuming only 60% of projected supply remained active by 2030. 6, 2025 report subsequently described Cathie Wood’s revised bullish target of $1.2 million, down from $1.5 million. Citing her CNBC interview, the report said stablecoins were taking part of the payments and savings role ARK had previously expected Bitcoin to serve in emerging markets. ViaBTC’s Ko sees accumulation alongside complacent positioning Commenting on recent market conditions, Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC, described Bitcoin’s trading as volatile but relatively constructive in comments to the publication. “I think market positioning remains somewhat complacent, and it looks like an accumulation period,” Ko said. According to Ko, funding rates remained positive while open interest had partially recovered from its September lows. He said Bitcoin had reclaimed its 50-week moving average and held above it for four to five weeks, a development he described as encouraging. In the same assessment, Ko said Bitcoin briefly recovered toward $84,000 before slipping below $80,000.

sources.title: JPMorgan names bitcoin top long-term return asset, urges caution on adding it to diversified portfolios
passages: 20, blockchain media outlet U.Today reported that JPMorgan, in its "2027 Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions" report, assessed bitcoin's future annualised compound return at 10.0 percent.

Combined with the latest long-term expected return outlook, it amounts to JPMorgan signalling to the market that it sees bitcoin not as a short-term volatile asset but as one of the targets for long-term asset allocation.The point to watch is whether actual fund flows will follow the outlook.

Matt Hougan (맷 호건), chief investment officer at Bitwise, said JPMorgan has moved from a sceptical stance on bitcoin to a stage where it is releasing long-term performance projections.JPMorgan cited expanding capital expenditure worldwide as the backdrop for the outlook.
JPMorgan said investors still view gold more optimistically than bitcoin.

It said a $15 trillion global capital expenditure boom, centred on technology investment including artificial intelligence, could drive economic growth and productivity gains over the next decade and support solid asset returns.
It projected stronger growth in advanced economies and improvements in bond returns and diversification opportunities.It also compared the investment appeal of bitcoin and gold.

extraction.body: J.P. Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term return forecasts for the first time, projecting that it will deliver a higher compound annual return than gold and U.S. large-cap stocks over the next 10–15 years. According to Wu Blockchain, JPMorgan Chase’s investment arm set its expected compound annual return for Bitcoin at 10% under its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions . This puts Bitcoin ahead of traditional investment assets in the forecasts it released. In the same set of forecasts, the expected compound annual return was 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 8.2% for U.S. real estate investment trusts. The projected rate for Bitcoin is 4.5 percentage points higher than gold’s and 2.5 percentage points higher than that of U.S. large-cap stocks. The comparison reflects expectations for a 10–15-year investment period rather than a price target for a single year. The firm estimated Bitcoin’s annualized volatility at 55% . This indicates that strong price swings may accompany its long-term return expectations. The arithmetic annual return expectation in the forecast set is 20.9%. The arithmetic average represents the average of periodic returns, while compound return reflects the investment’s cumulative growth rate over time; the two rates therefore represent different calculation methods. Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan interpreted these figures as a picture that places Bitcoin as the asset with the highest expected return over the next decade. JPMorgan’s inclusion of Bitcoin in these long-term forecasts for the first time also makes it possible to compare it directly with traditional assets, in addition to its price outlook. coreStoryFacts.text: 20, blockchain media outlet U.Today reported that JPMorgan, in its "2027 Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions" report, assessed bitcoin's future annualised compound return at 10.0 percent.

Combined with the latest long-term expected return outlook, it amounts to JPMorgan signalling to the market that it sees bitcoin not as a short-term volatile asset but as one of the targets for long-term asset allocation.The point to watch is whether actual fund flows will follow the outlook.

Matt Hougan (맷 호건), chief investment officer at Bitwise, said JPMorgan has moved from a sceptical stance on bitcoin to a stage where it is releasing long-term performance projections.JPMorgan cited expanding capital expenditure worldwide as the backdrop for the outlook.
JPMorgan said investors still view gold more optimistically than bitcoin.

It said a $15 trillion global capital expenditure boom, centred on technology investment including artificial intelligence, could drive economic growth and productivity gains over the next decade and support solid asset returns.
It projected stronger growth in advanced economies and improvements in bond returns and diversification opportunities.It also compared the investment appeal of bitcoin and gold.

Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term return forecasts for the first time, projecting that it will deliver a higher compound annual return than gold and U.S. large-cap stocks over the next 10–15 years.
This puts Bitcoin ahead of traditional investment assets in the forecasts it released.
The firm estimated Bitcoin’s annualized volatility at 55% .

It said a $15 trillion global capital expenditure boom, centred on technology investment including artificial intelligence, could drive economic growth and productivity gains over the next decade and support solid asset returns.
It projected stronger growth in advanced economies and improvements in bond returns and diversification opportunities.It also compared the investment appeal of bitcoin and gold.

In its “2027 Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions” report, the bank put bitcoin’s expected annualised compound return at 10.0 percent, above projections for U.S. REITs, small- and large-cap stocks, emerging-market equities and gold. It also compared investor sentiment and spot ETF flows between bitcoin and gold.

extraction.body: J.P. Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term return forecasts for the first time, projecting that it will deliver a higher compound annual return than gold and U.S. large-cap stocks over the next 10–15 years. According to Wu Blockchain, JPMorgan Chase’s investment arm set its expected compound annual return for Bitcoin at 10% under its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions . This puts Bitcoin ahead of traditional investment assets in the forecasts it released. In the same set of forecasts, the expected compound annual return was 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 8.2% for U.S. real estate investment trusts. The projected rate for Bitcoin is 4.5 percentage points higher than gold’s and 2.5 percentage points higher than that of U.S. large-cap stocks. The comparison reflects expectations for a 10–15-year investment period rather than a price target for a single year. The firm estimated Bitcoin’s annualized volatility at 55% . This indicates that strong price swings may accompany its long-term return expectations. The arithmetic annual return expectation in the forecast set is 20.9%. The arithmetic average represents the average of periodic returns, while compound return reflects the investment’s cumulative growth rate over time; the two rates therefore represent different calculation methods. Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan interpreted these figures as a picture that places Bitcoin as the asset with the highest expected return over the next decade. JPMorgan’s inclusion of Bitcoin in these long-term forecasts for the first time also makes it possible to compare it directly with traditional assets, in addition to its price outlook. sources.title: Adobe Emergency Patch For ColdFusion and Campaign Classic After Discovery of Seven Maximum-Severity Vulnerabilities - LinkedIn
passages: Dropping seven distinct CVSS 10.0 vulnerabilities in a single emergency update cycle is a massive wake-up call for enterprise security teams.

The real story here goes beyond the immediate data plumbing of patching old ColdFusion or Campaign Classic instances; it’s about the massive paradigm shift in how vulnerabilities are being discovered and weaponized.

Adobe openly moving to a twice-monthly patch schedule because frontier AI models are drastically compressing the window between public disclosure and exploitation changes the entire risk-management playbook.
When attackers can automate the process of reverse-engineering a patch within hours instead of days, the traditional timeline for enterprise deployment is completely broken.

Securing modern infrastructure is no longer an item you can safely forecast for the next scheduled maintenance window—it requires an agile, automated approach to asset discovery and immediate patch execution.
Excellent write-up on a critical turning point for application security! 🛡️🤖

The July security release fixes seven maximum-severity vulnerabilities—six in Adobe ColdFusion and one in Adobe Campaign Classic—that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems without requiring authentication or user interaction.

Although Adobe says it has not detected active exploitation of any of the newly disclosed vulnerabilities, the company has assigned the updates its highest deployment priority, recommending administrators install them within 72 hours.
Adobe has released an urgent series of security patches addressing multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting its ColdFusion application server and Campaign Classic marketing platform.
Internet-facing deployments should be updated immediately due to the ease with which attackers could potentially exploit the flaws.
That's what turns a vulnerability into an operational priority.

ColdFusion has a long history of becoming a target after critical vulnerabilities are disclosed, so this is one of those updates where waiting for evidence of widespread exploitation isn't a strategy.
Reducing exposure before attackers have an opportunity is almost always the better path.
The most serious issues patched in the release affect Adobe ColdFusion 2025 Update 9 and earlier, as well as ColdFusion 2023 Update 20 and earlier.

ColdFusion has historically remained a frequent target for cybercriminals due to its deployment in enterprise environments and the high value of the data often processed by applications built on the platform.

Over the past several years, multiple ColdFusion vulnerabilities have been weaponized shortly after disclosure, leading many organizations to treat every critical ColdFusion update as an emergency maintenance event.
The revised schedule is intended to improve the company's ability to deliver security fixes more rapidly as vulnerability discovery continues to accelerate across the software industry.
Adobe also confirmed that it will continue issuing emergency out-of-band updates whenever actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities or other critical threats require immediate action.

The vulnerabilities affect enterprise software widely used by government agencies, financial institutions, healthcare providers, educational organizations, and large businesses to power web applications and customer engagement platforms.
Like the ColdFusion vulnerabilities, exploitation does not require user interaction, increasing the potential risk for exposed systems.
Alongside the security release, Adobe announced a significant change to its vulnerability disclosure process aimed at reducing the time between vulnerability discovery and customer remediation.
Earlier this year, the company released emergency fixes for a zero-day vulnerability affecting Acrobat Reader that had reportedly been exploited in targeted attacks dating back several months.
Multiple Adobe flaws have also been linked to ransomware campaigns targeting government agencies and private-sector organizations.
ColdFusion has repeatedly appeared in incident response investigations involving ransomware operators and financially motivated cybercriminal groups.

Organizations operating ColdFusion servers restrict administrative interfaces from public internet access, enforce network segmentation, monitor application logs for suspicious activity, and deploy security updates immediately following release.
Adobe emphasized that the issue impacts only customer-managed on-premises deployments, including hybrid environments where Campaign components operate within an organization's infrastructure.
Adobe-hosted Campaign instances have already received the necessary security updates and require no customer action.
Beginning July 14, 2026, Adobe will transition from publishing security bulletins once each month to issuing them twice monthly, on the second and fourth Tuesday of every month.
Adobe has continued to issue regular security updates throughout 2026 across its enterprise software portfolio.

Adobe has released an urgent series of security patches addressing multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting its ColdFusion application server and Campaign Classic marketing platform. Internet-facing deployments should be updated immediately due to the ease with which attackers could potentially exploit the flaws. The July security release fixes seven maximum-severity vulnerabilities—six in Adobe ColdFusion and one in Adobe Campaign Classic—that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems without requiring authentication or user interaction. Although Adobe says it has not detected active exploitation of any of the newly disclosed vulnerabilities, the company has assigned the updates its highest deployment priority, recommending administrators install them within 72 hours. The vulnerabilities affect enterprise software widely used by government agencies, financial institutions, healthcare providers, educational organizations, and large businesses to power web applications and customer engagement platforms. Because many ColdFusion servers are accessible over the internet, security researchers have historically warned that newly disclosed remote code execution flaws often become attractive targets for cybercriminals shortly after technical details become public. The most serious issues patched in the release affect Adobe ColdFusion 2025 Update 9 and earlier, as well as ColdFusion 2023 Update 20 and earlier. CVE-2026-48281: An Improper Input Validation vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user. coreStoryFacts.text: Adobe released an update that closes eight critical vulnerabilities in Campaign Classic, four of which carry a 9.9 score on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System.
Successful attacks against these flaws would let an intruder run arbitrary code, slip past security controls, or climb to higher privileges inside the platform.
No exploits exist in the wild yet, so operators have a window to patch.
The authorization bug, CVE-2026-105780, deserves separate attention.
Authorization governs what a signed-in operator is allowed to do, and a failure there hands a low-privilege user the reach of an administrator.
Adobe rates the impact as full code execution, which puts it in the same tier as the injection flaws.
Adobe publishes its security bulletins at the Adobe Security Bulletins page , where you can track additional advisories for Campaign Classic and Connect.
Adobe also fixed a critical code injection flaw, CVE-2026-48360, carrying a 9.6 score in Adobe Connect Desktop and Mobile across Windows, macOS, and Android.
Exploitation leads to arbitrary code execution on the machine running the client.
Campaign Classic runs high-volume email and cross-channel marketing for enterprises, and it holds subscriber lists, campaign templates, and delivery logs.
That combination makes an injection hole in the product a direct route to customer data.
The vulnerabilities affect Adobe Campaign Classic version 7.4.4 build 9402 and earlier on Windows and Linux.
The reflected cross-site scripting flaw runs script in a victim's browser after they open a crafted link, and Adobe maps it to privilege escalation.
The realistic path is a phishing message aimed at a campaign operator who already holds a session in the administration console.
A desktop client with a code execution bug gives an attacker a foothold on a laptop, which is the starting point for credential theft and lateral movement across a corporate network.

Adobe has released an urgent series of security patches addressing multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting its ColdFusion application server and Campaign Classic marketing platform. Internet-facing deployments should be updated immediately due to the ease with which attackers could potentially exploit the flaws.

The vulnerabilities affect enterprise software widely used by government agencies, financial institutions, healthcare providers, educational organizations, and large businesses to power web applications and customer engagement platforms. Because many ColdFusion servers are accessible over the internet, security researchers have historically warned that newly disclosed remote code execution flaws often become attractive targets for cybercriminals shortly after technical details become public.
The most serious issues patched in the release affect Adobe ColdFusion 2025 Update 9 and earlier, as well as ColdFusion 2023 Update 20 and earlier.

CVE-2026-48282: An Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user. Exploitation of this issue does not require user interaction.

These classes of vulnerabilities are particularly dangerous because they can allow attackers to upload malicious payloads, bypass application controls, or manipulate file paths to gain control over vulnerable servers.

sources.title: Google tells platforms to noindex link-shared pages by default - PPC Land
passages: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.
The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain .
RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.
The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change.

Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.
For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost.

Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time.
The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows.
It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services.
The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top.
The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues.

It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for.
According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms.

Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?"
The question of manual actions has been live for weeks.
The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment.
That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content.
Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links.
Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition.
Those signals remain, now from third place down.
Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults?
The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page. The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed. The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property. Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." In the previous version, the monitoring list opened with spam signals such as redirects, large numbers of ad sections, spammy keywords and large blocks of encoded JavaScript, and Search Console was not mentioned anywhere on the page. Those signals remain, now from third place down. The changelog entry is brief. Under "What," Google wrote that it "Updated the user-generated spam prevention guide with guidance on blocking indexing of link-shared content and monitoring abuse in Search Console." The "Why" line says the change was made "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier." The phrase "link-shared content" appears in the changelog but not on the guide itself, which speaks of "shareable pages" and "direct sharing." The entry offers no figures on the scale of the abuse, no examples and no date for any related enforcement. It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document. The page remains a set of recommendations addressed to site and platform operators. The new section gives platforms two mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable. A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage. It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index. sources.title: Google's New AI Spam Detector Judges Networks, Not Pages — High-AI Sites Are Already Slipping - CMSWire
passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

A newly published Google research paper suggests the answer is yes, just not in the way most marketers expected.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment.
That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content.

Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition.
Those signals remain, now from third place down.
Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults?
The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

extraction.body: Web app builders and generated-content tools now sit in the spam guide, next to new Search Console alerts. Will those platforms switch their indexing defaults? Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist. The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp. Google has a help page for websites that let the public post things, and today it said that tools where people make pages, apps or automatically generated content to share by link can be abused by spammers too. Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The revised sentence reads: "Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web." Two edits sit inside that sentence. The first adds a category of service defined by what its users can publish - shared pages, generated content and web apps - rather than by whether it sells hosting. The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page. The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed. The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property. Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." In the previous version, the monitoring list opened with spam signals such as redirects, large numbers of ad sections, spammy keywords and large blocks of encoded JavaScript, and Search Console was not mentioned anywhere on the page. Those signals remain, now from third place down. The changelog entry is brief. Under "What," Google wrote that it "Updated the user-generated spam prevention guide with guidance on blocking indexing of link-shared content and monitoring abuse in Search Console." The "Why" line says the change was made "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier." The phrase "link-shared content" appears in the changelog but not on the guide itself, which speaks of "shareable pages" and "direct sharing." The entry offers no figures on the scale of the abuse, no examples and no date for any related enforcement. It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document. The page remains a set of recommendations addressed to site and platform operators. The new section gives platforms two mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable. A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage. It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index. Google's John Mueller explained in September 2024 that pages blocked by robots.txt can still be indexed when other pages link to them, and that a crawler shut out by robots.txt never sees a noindex tag on the blocked page. The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule. That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content. A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content. The new section does not discuss the interaction. It also differs in emphasis from another Search Central page revised five days earlier: on October 21, Google's "Control what you share with Google Search" page listed robots.txt as a blocking method only for images and videos , not as a way to keep web pages out of results. The remainder of the guide predates today's revision. It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content. The concern is the use of a platform's domain to publish spam rather than ranking damage to the host: in January, Mueller said that spam links in blog comments have no effect on a host site's rankings . Other recommendations are untouched: a published abuse policy communicated at sign-up; records of signup patterns such as form completion time, request volumes from one IP address range, user agents and chosen user names; manual approval of suspicious interactions; IP blocklists and firewall deny lists, with Akismet named as an option for WordPress; and reCAPTCHA or similar verification at sign-up to keep automated scripts from generating large numbers of sites. The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2. Google does not say which services prompted the change. PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language. Chat transcripts are one. When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached. Duck.ai's share pages instruct search engines not to index them in both the page markup and the server response, the two noindex methods that Google's new section lists, and they expire after 48 hours by default. Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records. Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths. App builders are another. Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain . RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains. Google's own products fall within the categories as well. Opal, its no-code app builder, expanded from 15 to more than 160 countries in November 2025 , drawing criticism from independent publisher advocate Nate Hake, who argued that promoting mass-generated blog and marketing content conflicted with Google's own Search guidance. Playground, the game builder Google opened to US adults on October 7, 2026, lets creators share games by link or publish them to a public gallery . Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines. Search Engine Roundtable , which reported the change today, described the new section as a significant addition that tells platforms to distinguish between content intended for public discovery and content intended only for direct access. According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms. SEO consultant Lily Ray wrote on X : "My first thought was Claude artifacts, ChatGPT pages/sites, FB posts, and other social/AI tools that make it easy to churn out indexable UGC at scale. Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?" Both readings remain speculation. Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable. What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results. The question of manual actions has been live for weeks. On October 7, Haynes reported a sharp rise in requests for help with manual actions, from essentially none to several a week, as Google's September 2026 spam update ran for 13 days and 16 hours before finishing on October 8. The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment. That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 . The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change. It gives approved forum and social platforms a dedicated pipeline to send new public posts and engagement signals to Google, on condition that they run active moderation and a user reporting mechanism, and that every post is tied to a creator with a public profile. Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched. Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes. Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link. If platforms adopt noindex as the default for such pages, content created there will not enter Google's index unless the platform provides, and the user selects, a way to make it public. Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like. For publishers and SEO teams, the change concerns the supply side of search spam. Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links. Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition. The guide's warning applies to every such service, whatever its current defaults. For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost. Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time. The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows. It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services. And it leaves a commercial tension unexamined: many platforms have grown in part through user pages that rank in Google, and the line between a page "meant for Search" and one made "for direct sharing" is drawn by the platform, not by Google. The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them. What: Google revised its guide to preventing user-generated spam. It now names tools for shared pages, generated content and web apps as open to abuse, adds an "Only index content meant for Search" section recommending noindex (via robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag) or a robots.txt block by default for pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility, and adds Search Console verification, report checks and platform-level creation and indexing alerts to its monitoring advice. When: Today, October 26, 2026, according to Google's documentation changelog and the page's "Last updated" stamp. Where: On the "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform" page in the Search Central documentation, under monitoring and debugging, with the monitoring tools located in Search Console.
