The second changes the unit of abuse from "sites" to "pages or sites," which brings individual URLs, not just whole sites, within the scope of the warning. Google names no products, companies or technologies. The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.

The new section, "Only index content meant for Search," is placed after the advice on identifying spammy accounts and before the passage on manual approval. It runs to two short paragraphs. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link."

"When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default."

Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed.

The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. The reference to subdomains is specific. Many hosting and app-building services give each user project its own subdomain, and a subdomain can be verified as a separate Search Console property.

Neither item comes with a threshold. Google does not say what size of spike warrants attention, or what share of indexable URLs counts as "large." In the previous version, the monitoring list opened with spam signals such as redirects, large numbers of ad sections, spammy keywords and large blocks of encoded JavaScript, and Search Console was not mentioned anywhere on the page. Those signals remain, now from third place down.

The changelog entry is brief. Under "What," Google wrote that it "Updated the user-generated spam prevention guide with guidance on blocking indexing of link-shared content and monitoring abuse in Search Console." The "Why" line says the change was made "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier."

The phrase "link-shared content" appears in the changelog but not on the guide itself, which speaks of "shareable pages" and "direct sharing." The entry offers no figures on the scale of the abuse, no examples and no date for any related enforcement. It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document. The page remains a set of recommendations addressed to site and platform operators.
The new section gives platforms two mechanisms, and they are not interchangeable.

A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage. It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index. Google's John Mueller explained in September 2024 that pages blocked by robots.txt can still be indexed when other pages link to them, and that a crawler shut out by robots.txt never sees a noindex tag on the blocked page. The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.

That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content. A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content. The new section does not discuss the interaction. It also differs in emphasis from another Search Central page revised five days earlier: on October 21, Google's "Control what you share with Google Search" page listed robots.txt as a blocking method only for images and videos , not as a way to keep web pages out of results.

The remainder of the guide predates today's revision. It still suggests applying a noindex robots meta tag to posts from new users who have no reputation on a platform, lifting it once they earn one, and adding a "nofollow or ugc rel attribute" to links in untrusted content. The concern is the use of a platform's domain to publish spam rather than ranking damage to the host: in January, Mueller said that spam links in blog comments have no effect on a host site's rankings .

Other recommendations are untouched: a published abuse policy communicated at sign-up; records of signup patterns such as form completion time, request volumes from one IP address range, user agents and chosen user names; manual approval of suspicious interactions; IP blocklists and firewall deny lists, with Akismet named as an option for WordPress; and reCAPTCHA or similar verification at sign-up to keep automated scripts from generating large numbers of sites. The monitoring section still cites the site: search operator, Google Alerts, web server logs, the Google Safe Browsing API and language detection tools, including the Google Translate API v2.
Google does not say which services prompted the change. PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

Chat transcripts are one. When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached. Duck.ai's share pages instruct search engines not to index them in both the page markup and the server response, the two noindex methods that Google's new section lists, and they expire after 48 hours by default. Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records. Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.

App builders are another. Research by security firm RedAccess, reported in May 2026, found more than 5,000 apps built with vibe coding tools such as Lovable, Replit, Base44 and Netlify that had essentially no authentication, along with phishing sites impersonating Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe's and McDonald's on Lovable's domain . RedAccess located the apps by searching Google and Bing for the platforms' default domains.

Google's own products fall within the categories as well. Opal, its no-code app builder, expanded from 15 to more than 160 countries in November 2025 , drawing criticism from independent publisher advocate Nate Hake, who argued that promoting mass-generated blog and marketing content conflicted with Google's own Search guidance. Playground, the game builder Google opened to US adults on October 7, 2026, lets creators share games by link or publish them to a public gallery . Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.

Search Engine Roundtable , which reported the change today, described the new section as a significant addition that tells platforms to distinguish between content intended for public discovery and content intended only for direct access. According to Search Engine Roundtable, consultant Marie Haynes asked on X whether the update means new manual actions are coming for AI tools and app-building platforms.

SEO consultant Lily Ray wrote on X : "My first thought was Claude artifacts, ChatGPT pages/sites, FB posts, and other social/AI tools that make it easy to churn out indexable UGC at scale. Another clue from Google about new types of spam they are dealing with (likely at a big enough scale to warrant changing their documentation) and ... another clue about what they'll be targeting in the future?"

Both readings remain speculation. Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable. What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.

The question of manual actions has been live for weeks. On October 7, Haynes reported a sharp rise in requests for help with manual actions, from essentially none to several a week, as Google's September 2026 spam update ran for 13 days and 16 hours before finishing on October 8. The evidence was anecdotal, and Google did not comment. That update was the fourth spam update of the year, following rollouts on March 24, June 24 and August 18 .

The UGC Fresh Data Program offers a contrast with today's change. It gives approved forum and social platforms a dedicated pipeline to send new public posts and engagement signals to Google, on condition that they run active moderation and a user reporting mechanism, and that every post is tied to a creator with a public profile. Within one month, then, Google has documented a faster route into its systems for moderated public discussion, and a default route out of its index for user-created pages that were never meant to be searched.

Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes. Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link. If platforms adopt noindex as the default for such pages, content created there will not enter Google's index unless the platform provides, and the user selects, a way to make it public. Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

For publishers and SEO teams, the change concerns the supply side of search spam. Pages published on trusted platform domains can compete in results with original sites, and since May those same spam policies have applied to the AI answers that sit above the links. Platforms that tighten indexing defaults reduce one source of that competition. The guide's warning applies to every such service, whatever its current defaults.

For platform operators, the monitoring additions carry a cost. Verifying subdomains, watching Page Indexing reports for unexplained growth, and building internal alerts for concentrated URL creation by a handful of accounts all require engineering and moderation time. The guide acknowledges this kind of trade-off elsewhere, noting that moderation "adds overhead" to daily workflows. It does not quantify what Google expects of smaller services. And it leaves a commercial tension unexamined: many platforms have grown in part through user pages that rank in Google, and the line between a page "meant for Search" and one made "for direct sharing" is drawn by the platform, not by Google.

Who: Google, through its Search Central documentation, addressing operators of hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content or web apps. The change also concerns publishers, SEO teams and marketers who build on those platforms or compete with pages hosted on them.

What: Google revised its guide to preventing user-generated spam. It now names tools for shared pages, generated content and web apps as open to abuse, adds an "Only index content meant for Search" section recommending noindex (via robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag) or a robots.txt block by default for pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility, and adds Search Console verification, report checks and platform-level creation and indexing alerts to its monitoring advice.
When: Today, October 26, 2026, according to Google's documentation changelog and the page's "Last updated" stamp.
Where: On the "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform" page in the Search Central documentation, under monitoring and debugging, with the monitoring tools located in Search Console.

Why: According to Google, "To help platforms keep user-created pages that aren't meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier." Google has not said which services prompted the change or whether enforcement will follow.

sources.title: Google's New AI Spam Detector Judges Networks, Not Pages — High-AI Sites Are Already Slipping - CMSWire
passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.
At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters.
SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism.
Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

extraction.body: CMSWire's Marketing & Customer Experience Leadership channel is the go-to hub for actionable research, editorial and opinion for CMOs, aspiring CMOs and today's customer experience innovators. Our dedicated editorial and research teams focus on bringing you the data and information you need to navigate today's complex customer, organizational and technical landscapes. We've got you covered. For two years the AI content debate has circled one question: can Google actually tell? A newly published Google research paper suggests the answer is yes, just not in the way most marketers expected. The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System. Google built it to fight AI-generated video spam on its platforms, but the methods it describes (text embeddings, template detection, publishing-behavior analysis) apply just as cleanly to web content. Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions. The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving. Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search. This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out. Correlation is not causation. But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention. Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time. Is this page thin? Does it satisfy intent? Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model. Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same. At volume, that flood is built to swamp content-level filters. S-CTS works from a wider angle. It looks for the organizational structure of a spam operation, meaning the mass reuse of a semantic narrative template across many accounts, combined with infrastructure signals suggesting those accounts share an operator. The system groups related accounts into what the researchers call Generation Clusters, networks statistically likely to be running the same script, API or automation stack. Two components do the work. A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces. An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source. When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages. Now swap "accounts" for "domains" and "videos" for "articles." A network of sites publishing 30 templated posts a day from the same prompt stack fits this detection model exactly. S-CTS groups accounts that share templated content and infrastructure signals into Generation Clusters, then removes the entire cluster at once instead of penalizing individual pages. For SEO practitioners, the most useful detail sits in the methodology: Sentence-BERT. The researchers cite SBERT, a model that converts sentences into embeddings comparable by cosine similarity, to support the paper's core assumption that automated AI text leaves a distinct mathematical footprint. When thousands of pages come from the same prompts and the same tools, they land close together in embedding space no matter how different they look to a human reader. SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism. Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently. One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation. The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models. That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining. When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately. Sentence-BERT converts text into embeddings, and pages generated from the same prompts and tools cluster together in embedding space even when their wording looks unique to a human reader. The loudest reaction to this research has also been the least accurate one, so the distinction is worth stating plainly. Google's official guidance from 2023 still stands: content gets rewarded for quality and helpfulness regardless of how it was produced. Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts. What Google targets falls under its spam policies , specifically scaled content abuse: producing large volumes of pages mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help people. The March 2024 core update already wiped out networks of AI-heavy sites under that policy. This research shows the enforcement machinery getting sharper. The practical line is velocity and intent. A brand publishing four edited, AI-assisted articles a week that answer real customer questions looks nothing like a site pushing 30 posts a day from one prompt template. The second pattern is a fingerprint, and fingerprints are what cluster-level detection finds. When a skeptic in Gabe's replies asked whether these systems would sweep up all AI-generated content, his answer was direct: Google uses multiple signals, AI usage alone does not equal spam and anyone scaling thin content with AI should consider themselves warned. No. Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings. The following table highlights the most important lessons, actions and strategic considerations emerging from these five recommended content moves. Prioritizing human-led writing, stripping templated AI phrasing, cutting padding, adding real point of view and publishing at least some content for readers rather than rankings all reduce the templated-content fingerprint S-CTS looks for. The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape. The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality. The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network. That is a much harder problem to solve with a plugin or a prompt, and based on the traffic declines of the past month, Google may already be grading the exam. My own strategy stays the same: build a strong brand on a strong domain, publish content that serves real search intent and treat AI as a tool rather than an identity. S-CTS groups accounts that share templated content and infrastructure signals into Generation Clusters, then removes the entire cluster at once instead of penalizing individual pages.
For SEO practitioners, the most useful detail sits in the methodology: Sentence-BERT.

The researchers cite SBERT, a model that converts sentences into embeddings comparable by cosine similarity, to support the paper's core assumption that automated AI text leaves a distinct mathematical footprint. When thousands of pages come from the same prompts and the same tools, they land close together in embedding space no matter how different they look to a human reader.

SBERT has existed since 2019, and Montti points out the SEO industry has rarely discussed it as a spam-detection mechanism. Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.

One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation. The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models. That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining. When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
Sentence-BERT converts text into embeddings, and pages generated from the same prompts and tools cluster together in embedding space even when their wording looks unique to a human reader.
The loudest reaction to this research has also been the least accurate one, so the distinction is worth stating plainly.

Google's official guidance from 2023 still stands: content gets rewarded for quality and helpfulness regardless of how it was produced. Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
What Google targets falls under its spam policies , specifically scaled content abuse: producing large volumes of pages mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help people.
The March 2024 core update already wiped out networks of AI-heavy sites under that policy. This research shows the enforcement machinery getting sharper.

The practical line is velocity and intent. A brand publishing four edited, AI-assisted articles a week that answer real customer questions looks nothing like a site pushing 30 posts a day from one prompt template. The second pattern is a fingerprint, and fingerprints are what cluster-level detection finds.

When a skeptic in Gabe's replies asked whether these systems would sweep up all AI-generated content, his answer was direct: Google uses multiple signals, AI usage alone does not equal spam and anyone scaling thin content with AI should consider themselves warned.

No. Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
The following table highlights the most important lessons, actions and strategic considerations emerging from these five recommended content moves.

Prioritizing human-led writing, stripping templated AI phrasing, cutting padding, adding real point of view and publishing at least some content for readers rather than rankings all reduce the templated-content fingerprint S-CTS looks for.

The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape. The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality. The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network. That is a much harder problem to solve with a plugin or a prompt, and based on the traffic declines of the past month, Google may already be grading the exam.

My own strategy stays the same: build a strong brand on a strong domain, publish content that serves real search intent and treat AI as a tool rather than an identity. The sites getting removed at the cluster level made themselves look like machines. Do not be one of them.

Google has recently created an additional “Only index content meant for Search” section within the spam guide it updated on Oct. 26. The new section advises websites with pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility to set a noindex tag or use a robots.txt directive to block crawlers by default for those pages. According to Google’s changelog this is an addition relating to “blocking indexing of link-shared content.” The new section includes a link to the introductory page about robots.txt , and according to that introductory page the robots.txt file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Google’s new “Only index content meant for Search” section follows the guide’s advice on spotting spammy accounts and reads: “If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.” “When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.” The guide’s opening paragraph said hosting platforms “may be similarly open to abuse.” The updated sentence adds “tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps,” and says spammers may create a large number of “pages or sites” where it used to say sites. The previous version, last updated Dec. 10, 2025, already suggested noindex on posts from new users until they build a reputation on the platform. That advice is unchanged. Google’s robots.txt introduction says a page “that’s disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites.” Google won’t crawl the blocked content in that case, but the URL and possibly the anchor text of links pointing to it can appear in results, without a description. Google’s page on noindex says the rule only works when robots.txt isn’t blocking the page, because otherwise “the crawler will never see the noindex rule.” Google’s “Control what you share” page , updated Oct. 21, lists robots.txt as applicable to “images and video” and noindex as applicable to “all content types.” On July 27, I confirmed that Claude’s share path was blocked by a “Disallow” directive in robots.txt. In addition, the share pages also returned a “none” value for the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header. Google treats “none” as equal to both noindex and nofollow according to its documentation of robots meta tags . I have been unable to determine what Google saw when it initially found those links. The new spam guide from Google states you should be verifying your website or subdomain through Search Console for your platform to receive emails when it gets a manual action or has a security issue. It further suggests you check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report on an ongoing basis for “unexpected spikes” of indexed pages, impressions or queries which do not align with your platform’s intent. A new bullet under the guide’s monitoring advice suggests tracking creation and indexing at the platform level, with alerts for spikes in newly published public pages or “a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.” Google’s changelog says its Oct. 26 update to the spam guide aims to help platforms “keep user-created pages that aren’t meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier.” For share links, generated outputs, and app pages, check that any noindex can reach Googlebot. A robots.txt rule that blocks Googlebot from those pages means Google never reads it. The Page Indexing report that Google’s new monitoring advice points to has a status called “Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt.” Google’s help for that status says to remove the block and use noindex. Share URLs that Google indexes despite a robots.txt block can appear under that status in Search Console. Follow on YouTube. Matt G. A holding can be measured against the fixed maximum of 21 million coins or against the number of coins already in circulation, and the two measures give different results. A holding does not give a company control over Bitcoin. Independently operated full nodes enforce the network’s consensus rules, while miners assemble transactions into new blocks. Ownership and network governance remain separate. The largest holders are also exceptional cases. Many companies holding Bitcoin have smaller positions and do not return repeatedly to capital markets to fund purchases. Circulating supply refers to the coins that have already been mined, and the protocol caps the total at 21 million. Circulating supply, however, includes coins that may not have moved for years. Consider a company that acquires 1,000 BTC and transfers them from a trading venue into long-term custody. The coins remain part of circulating supply because the protocol has not destroyed or locked them. They are no longer resting in an active exchange order book, though. Analysts try to estimate liquid supply by examining wallet activity, but the results are imperfect. Selling additional common shares reduces existing investors’ percentage ownership, while convertible notes remain debt unless the conditions for conversion are met. The Bitcoin appears as an asset, but the financing behind the purchase still carries consequences. A board approving a Bitcoin reserve needs to decide how the asset will be held and who can authorize transfers. It also needs a process for verifying the balance. A purchase made from surplus cash does not carry the same fixed commitments as one financed with debt or preferred shares. Interest and dividend obligations continue even when Bitcoin falls in value. passages: Why Corporate Bitcoin Treasuries Are Becoming a Market Structure Story

Corporate Bitcoin holdings have become more than a balance-sheet detail. When a company places Bitcoin in its treasury, it reflects a financing decision that can last for years, and it can change where part of the asset’s supply is held.

Prices change by the second, while corporate disclosures show something different. Binance publishes a live bitcoin price that captures the market at a specific moment, while company filings describe how much Bitcoin a business holds and how it paid for it.

Bitcoin held as a treasury reserve is generally intended to remain on the balance sheet rather than respond to every short-term market move. A large position can therefore alter the distribution of ownership without changing the official circulating supply.

Percentages describing a company’s share of Bitcoin depend on the reference point. A holding can be measured against the fixed maximum of 21 million coins or against the number of coins already in circulation, and the two measures give different results.

A holding does not give a company control over Bitcoin. Independently operated full nodes enforce the network’s consensus rules, while miners assemble transactions into new blocks. Ownership and network governance remain separate. The largest holders are also exceptional cases. Many companies holding Bitcoin have smaller positions and do not return repeatedly to capital markets to fund purchases.

Circulating supply refers to the coins that have already been mined, and the protocol caps the total at 21 million. Circulating supply, however, includes coins that may not have moved for years. Consider a company that acquires 1,000 BTC and transfers them from a trading venue into long-term custody. The coins remain part of circulating supply because the protocol has not destroyed or locked them. They are no longer resting in an active exchange order book, though.

Analysts try to estimate liquid supply by examining wallet activity, but the results are imperfect. An inactive address could belong to a long-term holder, someone who has lost access or an owner waiting to sell. Available supply is only one influence on price. Existing holders can sell, demand can weaken and trading activity can expand. Corporate purchases may affect liquidity, but they cannot dictate the market’s response.

Some companies use cash generated through normal operations. Others sell common shares, convertible notes or preferred securities. Each method leaves different obligations after the Bitcoin enters custody.

Preferred stock is one source of capital some companies use. A company’s securities filings describe the terms of any such security and the risks that arise from its Bitcoin holdings. Preferred shares establish dividend and liquidation terms that do not apply to common stock.

A company that raises $100 million will not necessarily spend the full amount on Bitcoin. Fees take a portion, and some of the cash may remain available for operating costs. How the money was raised matters too. Selling additional common shares reduces existing investors’ percentage ownership, while convertible notes remain debt unless the conditions for conversion are met. The Bitcoin appears as an asset, but the financing behind the purchase still carries consequences.

A board approving a Bitcoin reserve needs to decide how the asset will be held and who can authorize transfers. It also needs a process for verifying the balance. Investors should know whether the company has pledged any coins as collateral.

Funding changes the risk. A purchase made from surplus cash does not carry the same fixed commitments as one financed with debt or preferred shares. Interest and dividend obligations continue even when Bitcoin falls in value.

Corporate treasurers are watching bonds as closely as bitcoin. Recent coverage of stocks dipping as Treasury yields hit multi-decade highs points to the rate backdrop that shapes whether companies hold cash, bonds or crypto.

Useful reporting includes the amount held, aggregate acquisition cost, outstanding financing and custody arrangements. These details show both the Bitcoin position and the obligations used to build it. Large reserves can also make a company’s reported results and share price more sensitive to Bitcoin, even when its original operating business has not changed.

U.S. accounting rules now make that sensitivity easier to see. Under an update the Financial Accounting Standards Board issued in December 2023, companies measure most crypto holdings at fair value, so swings in Bitcoin’s price flow directly into reported earnings each quarter instead of showing up only as impairment charges.
Audited accounts and repeated filings will matter more than the number of purchase announcements. They reveal whether companies are holding their positions, adding to them or reducing them.

Funding conditions will also shape what happens next. Companies may find repeated purchases harder to finance if investors demand larger returns or their shares trade less favorably. Stronger custody practices and clearer reporting may improve confidence without removing exposure to Bitcoin. Corporate treasuries have become a visible part of Bitcoin ownership, and their lasting importance will depend on how long those reserves remain in place and whether more companies adopt similar policies. They cannot set Bitcoin’s next price, but their decisions affect where part of its limited supply sits.

In May 2026, Binance Research estimated that approximately 18.5% of Bitcoin’s 21 million maximum supply was held by institutions, with public companies accounting for around 1.24 million BTC.
It also estimated that nearly half of all corporate Bitcoin accumulation at the time took place in the last year.
Loan agreements commonly require pledged assets to be worth well above the amount borrowed, and they set thresholds that trigger a call for more collateral or partial repayment.
If the ratio falls further and the shortfall is not remedied, the lender may be able to liquidate the collateral.
The risk is higher if businesses are borrowing heavily against large treasury positions.
This means the structure of a loan is as important as its size.
Anyone assessing a corporate Bitcoin strategy may want to look for conservative loan-to-value ratios and adequate liquidity reserves.
If companies are unable to do so, their pledged BTC may be liquidated, which could add to selling pressure in the market.
Corporate adoption has often been measured by the amount of Bitcoin companies purchase.
As more companies borrow against their holdings, purchases may no longer be the only way to measure Bitcoin’s institutional adoption.
It may increasingly be judged on BTC’s ability to serve the same financial purposes as other assets companies already borrow against.
Bitcoin appears to be becoming more institutional.
That can make collateralized lending easier to imagine than it was when retail wallets and crypto-native businesses dominated BTC ownership.
Those issues have not been eradicated, but the infrastructure around the asset has improved.
Institutional custodians can hold pledged Bitcoin, contracts can include margin requirements, and lenders can continuously track the value of the collateral.
Treasury assets may sit on a balance sheet without any activity, while collateral is an active part of the financial system.
Bitcoin-based borrowing establishes a direct link between market fluctuations and corporate liquidity.
Historically, Bitcoin has been challenging in that regard due to volatility, custody requirements and regulatory uncertainty.
That setup can resemble traditional collateralized lending, with one notable difference: the collateral is a digital asset that trades around the clock.

When a company places Bitcoin in its treasury, it reflects a financing decision that can last for years, and it can change where part of the asset’s supply is held. Prices change by the second, while corporate disclosures show something different. Binance publishes a live bitcoin price that captures the market at a specific moment, while company filings describe how much Bitcoin a business holds and how it paid for it. Bitcoin held as a treasury reserve is generally intended to remain on the balance sheet rather than respond to every short-term market move. A large position can therefore alter the distribution of ownership without changing the official circulating supply. Percentages describing a company’s share of Bitcoin depend on the reference point. A holding can be measured against the fixed maximum of 21 million coins or against the number of coins already in circulation, and the two measures give different results. A holding does not give a company control over Bitcoin. Independently operated full nodes enforce the network’s consensus rules, while miners assemble transactions into new blocks. Ownership and network governance remain separate. The largest holders are also exceptional cases. Many companies holding Bitcoin have smaller positions and do not return repeatedly to capital markets to fund purchases. Circulating supply refers to the coins that have already been mined, and the protocol caps the total at 21 million. Circulating supply, however, includes coins that may not have moved for years. Consider a company that acquires 1,000 BTC and transfers them from a trading venue into long-term custody. The coins remain part of circulating supply because the protocol has not destroyed or locked them. They are no longer resting in an active exchange order book, though. Analysts try to estimate liquid supply by examining wallet activity, but the results are imperfect. An inactive address could belong to a long-term holder, someone who has lost access or an owner waiting to sell. Available supply is only one influence on price. Existing holders can sell, demand can weaken and trading activity can expand. Corporate purchases may affect liquidity, but they cannot dictate the market’s response. Some companies use cash generated through normal operations. Others sell common shares, convertible notes or preferred securities. Each method leaves different obligations after the Bitcoin enters custody. Preferred stock is one source of capital some companies use. A company’s securities filings describe the terms of any such security and the risks that arise from its Bitcoin holdings. Preferred shares establish dividend and liquidation terms that do not apply to common stock. A company that raises $100 million will not necessarily spend the full amount on Bitcoin. Fees take a portion, and some of the cash may remain available for operating costs. How the money was raised matters too. Selling additional common shares reduces existing investors’ percentage ownership, while convertible notes remain debt unless the conditions for conversion are met. The Bitcoin appears as an asset, but the financing behind the purchase still carries consequences. A board approving a Bitcoin reserve needs to decide how the asset will be held and who can authorize transfers. It also needs a process for verifying the balance. Investors should know whether the company has pledged any coins as collateral. Funding changes the risk. A purchase made from surplus cash does not carry the same fixed commitments as one financed with debt or preferred shares. Interest and dividend obligations continue even when Bitcoin falls in value. Corporate treasurers are watching bonds as closely as bitcoin. Recent coverage of stocks dipping as Treasury yields hit multi-decade highs points to the rate backdrop that shapes whether companies hold cash, bonds or crypto. Stronger custody practices and clearer reporting may improve confidence without removing exposure to Bitcoin. “iMac is the world’s best all-in-one, and today it raises the bar yet again,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering.

Featuring a faster CPU and GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, it blazes through everyday apps and multitasking while delivering powerful performance for creative workflows like photo and video editing.
For Intel-based upgraders, the leap is even greater, with up to 18x faster performance than the most popular Intel-based iMac.

It is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the stand, 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets, and 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards.
It is manufactured with 40 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain.
Apple Intelligence also makes apps smarter and more useful.

In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organize a user’s tabs into topics; notifies them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enables the creation of custom extensions based on a description.

In addition, users can easily create an automation in Shortcuts by simply describing it or tap into intelligent photo editing tools in the Photos app. iMac also supports a growing ecosystem of AI apps optimized for Apple silicon, including LM Studio Bionic and Topaz Studio, helping users learn faster, think in new ways, and get more done.
Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984.
Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro.

Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV.
The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.

extraction.body: Apple unveils new :br(s):iMac with M6, :br(s):delivering a major :br(s):boost in performance and AI capabilities With blazing-fast performance, enhanced connectivity, Siri AI, and macOS 27, all in a stunning design in seven vibrant colors, the world’s best all-in-one gets even better CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the new iMac featuring the superfast M6, delivering even more performance and powerful AI capabilities in its strikingly thin all-in-one design. From families and aspiring creators to small businesses, users will experience the speed and power of M6 in everything they do. Featuring a faster CPU and GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, it blazes through everyday apps and multitasking while delivering powerful performance for creative workflows like photo and video editing. For Intel-based upgraders, the leap is even greater, with up to 18x faster performance than the most popular Intel-based iMac. 1 And together with the Dual 16-core Neural Engine, the new iMac delivers up to 5x faster on-device AI performance than M4. 1 Whether users are taking advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features across apps and macOS, running local AI models, or vibe coding, iMac is a powerful platform for AI while preserving user privacy. 2 Connectivity gets even better with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, along with available 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet and storage that is up to 2x faster, so apps and large projects launch in an instant. 3 Completing the iMac experience is an expansive 24-inch 4.5K Retina display; an industry-leading camera, speakers, and mics; up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports; color-matched accessories; and the power of macOS 27. Available in a spectrum of seven colors — blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver — the new iMac is a tremendous upgrade for existing users and an incredible gateway into everything the Mac can do for new users. Customers can pre-order starting tomorrow, October 28, with availability beginning Friday, November 6. “iMac is the world’s best all-in-one, and today it raises the bar yet again,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With the blazing performance and AI capabilities of M6 supercharging every workflow and the next generation of Apple Intelligence with Siri AI — combined with its stunning 24-inch Retina display, its gorgeous design in seven vibrant colors, and macOS 27 — the new iMac has everything users need to run their businesses, manage their lives, and bring their ideas to life.” iMac with M6: A Huge Leap in Performance and AI Capabilities With M6, iMac brings even more performance, for everything from everyday productivity to creative workloads and AI tasks. iMac with M6 features up to a 12-core CPU — two more cores than before — delivering the world’s fastest single-threaded CPU performance. 4 Everything feels extra snappy and responsive for families managing busy calendars, students putting the finishing touches on a project, and small business owners running their companies. An up-to-12-core GPU, also with two more cores than before, now features Neural Accelerators in each core, delivering up to 2x faster graphics for more intensive tasks like photo editing, along with fantastic gaming performance compared to M4. 3 Students and creators can now fly through tasks like editing and sharing their latest videos or designing a project for class, all while multitasking with their favorite messaging or entertainment apps. The new Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers up to 2x faster AI compute than the previous generation, and combined with the advanced GPU and faster memory bandwidth and with higher memory bandwidth up to 170GB/s, iMac rips through AI tasks like running LLMs on device. 3 With all this performance packed into its stunning design, iMac is the perfect all-in-one for a wide range of users and workflows. Beyond delivering exceptional performance for everyday productivity and creative workflows, iMac is also a powerful platform for AI, enabling users to take advantage of advanced AI capabilities while protecting their privacy. With macOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence is deeply personal, seamlessly integrated across apps, and built with privacy from the ground up. Apple Intelligence powers Siri AI, a new version of Siri that is profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal, helping users get more done than ever before. On iMac, users can tap into Siri AI to ask questions; find what they need across their messages, emails, photos, and more; and take action across apps. Siri AI is built right into Spotlight, making it easy to search for answers on virtually any topic and ask follow-up questions. With the expansive 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, users can leverage Visual Intelligence with a dedicated keyboard shortcut to ask Siri about anything on their screen, from a chart in a spreadsheet to a photo in a browser tab. Users can also write and edit with Siri almost anywhere they type, and in Mail and Messages, Siri can reflect their typical style and tone. Apple Intelligence also makes apps smarter and more useful. In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organize a user’s tabs into topics; notifies them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enables the creation of custom extensions based on a description. In addition, users can easily create an automation in Shortcuts by simply describing it or tap into intelligent photo editing tools in the Photos app. iMac also supports a growing ecosystem of AI apps optimized for Apple silicon, including LM Studio Bionic and Topaz Studio, helping users learn faster, think in new ways, and get more done. Best-in-Class Connectivity and Faster Storage The new iMac features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, along with 2.5Gb Ethernet that delivers up to 2.5x faster wired connectivity than the previous generation. 5 This means faster transfers of large files, smoother streaming of high-resolution content, and even better performance for gaming and demanding business workflows. And with up to 2x faster SSD read and write performance, apps launch quickly, and large files like photo libraries and video projects load in an instant. 3 Up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports enable superfast data transfers and make it easy to connect a wide range of accessories, including external storage and docks. 6 Users can also connect up to two 6K external displays, creating a vast workspace with more than 50 million pixels to spread out their work. The new iMac is a tremendous upgrade — especially for users coming from an Intel-based iMac, who will experience performance that’s up to 18x faster. 1 And with macOS 27, Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features integrated across apps make AI tasks on iMac more personal and powerful than ever. iMac also includes all of the popular features and capabilities that make it the world’s best all-in-one: macOS 27 Golden Gate: An Unrivaled Experience The new iMac comes to life with macOS 27 . In addition to Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, iMac gets even more responsive, reliable, and delightful for everyday use with refinements to design, performance, search, and more. Updates to Liquid Glass deliver a more focused and approachable experience. A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined. The new iMac was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the stand, 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets, and 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards. It is manufactured with 40 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain. The new iMac meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled. Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it. The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.

Beyond delivering exceptional performance for everyday productivity and creative workflows, iMac is also a powerful platform for AI, enabling users to take advantage of advanced AI capabilities while protecting their privacy. macOS 27 Golden Gate: An Unrivaled Experience

Updates to Liquid Glass deliver a more focused and approachable experience. A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined.

The new iMac was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the stand, 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets, and 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards. It is manufactured with 40 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain. The new iMac meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled.

Apple Intelligence also makes apps smarter and more useful. In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organize a user’s tabs into topics; notifies them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enables the creation of custom extensions based on a description. In addition, users can easily create an automation in Shortcuts by simply describing it or tap into intelligent photo editing tools in the Photos app. iMac also supports a growing ecosystem of AI apps optimized for Apple silicon, including LM Studio Bionic and Topaz Studio, helping users learn faster, think in new ways, and get more done.
Best-in-Class Connectivity and Faster Storage

The new iMac features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, along with 2.5Gb Ethernet that delivers up to 2.5x faster wired connectivity than the previous generation. 5 This means faster transfers of large files, smoother streaming of high-resolution content, and even better performance for gaming and demanding business workflows. Up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports enable superfast data transfers and make it easy to connect a wide range of accessories, including external storage and docks. 6 Users can also connect up to two 6K external displays, creating a vast workspace with more than 50 million pixels to spread out their work.

The new iMac is a tremendous upgrade — especially for users coming from an Intel-based iMac, who will experience performance that’s up to 18x faster. 1 And with macOS 27, Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features integrated across apps make AI tasks on iMac more personal and powerful than ever.

The new iMac comes to life with macOS 27 . In addition to Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, iMac gets even more responsive, reliable, and delightful for everyday use with refinements to design, performance, search, and more. Updates to Liquid Glass deliver a more focused and approachable experience. A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined.

The new iMac was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the stand, 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets, and 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards. It is manufactured with 40 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain. The new iMac meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 10 and designed to be recycled.

Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.

sources.title: Robinhood Shares Fall 8.7% as Q3 Revenue Miss and Crypto Trading Decline Weigh on Outlook - Yahoo Finance
passages: Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading on Wednesday after the online brokerage reported third-quarter 2026 revenue below analyst expectations, despite exceeding adjusted earnings forecasts.
A substantial decline in cryptocurrency trading revenue, higher operating expenses and management's comments about fourth-quarter trading spreads contributed to the market reaction.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Following the pre-market decline, Robinhood shares were indicated at approximately $86.31.
Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55.
Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year.
Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook.
Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions.
The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs.
Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth.
The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results.

Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ:HOOD) shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading on Wednesday after the online brokerage reported third-quarter 2026 revenue below analyst expectations, despite exceeding adjusted earnings forecasts. A substantial decline in cryptocurrency trading revenue, higher operating expenses and management's comments about fourth-quarter trading spreads contributed to the market reaction. The stock fell towards $86.31 from its previous closing price of $94.56, following the release of quarterly results the previous evening. Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55. However, revenue of approximately $1.42 billion fell short of market expectations, while reported earnings under generally accepted accounting principles declined year over year. Robinhood's third-quarter results showed a difference between adjusted profitability and its reported financial performance. GAAP diluted earnings per share declined 16% from the corresponding quarter of 2025 to $0.51, also falling short of expectations. The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs. Investors focused on these pressures despite the adjusted earnings beat, contributing to the decline in the company's share price before the market opened. The cryptocurrency business was a significant source of weakness during the third quarter. Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year. Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions. The decline affected the company's overall financial performance, even as other trading categories recorded growth. Revenue from equities, options and event contracts increased during the period, providing some offset to the weaker cryptocurrency business. The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results. Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook. Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma indicated that trading spreads had narrowed at the beginning of the fourth quarter. The observation raised questions about the revenue Robinhood may generate from transaction activity during the final months of 2026. Narrower spreads can affect the amount of revenue earned from certain trading transactions, potentially reducing the company's effective take rate. The comments therefore added uncertainty to the outlook for transaction-based revenue following the third-quarter decline in cryptocurrency activity. Investors will monitor whether the tighter spreads persist and how they affect the company's financial performance during the fourth quarter. Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth. Operating costs rose 16% year over year, compared with a 12% increase in total revenue. Futures linked to the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average were little changed overnight, while Nasdaq futures recorded a modest increase. The difference between Robinhood's share price movement and the broader market suggested that the decline was primarily associated with the company's quarterly results and management commentary. The combination of weaker cryptocurrency revenue, higher expenses and uncertainty about trading spreads outweighed the positive adjusted earnings surprise. The Federal Reserve announcement will provide additional information about the interest rate environment heading into the final months of 2026. Following the pre-market decline, Robinhood shares were indicated at approximately $86.31. That level remained above the company's reported 52-week low of $63.52 but substantially below its 52-week high of $150.47. The latest movement followed a quarter in which the company reported higher overall revenue but weaker cryptocurrency trading activity and a decline in GAAP earnings per share. The share price reaction also reflected management's comments about tighter trading spreads at the start of the fourth quarter. The company's subsequent performance will depend partly on trading activity, transaction revenue and its ability to manage operating costs. Robinhood reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the $0.55 consensus estimate, while revenue of approximately $1.42 billion fell below market forecasts. Cryptocurrency transaction revenue declined 55% to $120 million, accompanied by a 38% reduction in trading volume. Operating expenses increased 16%, outpacing the company's 12% revenue growth, while GAAP diluted earnings per share fell 16% to $0.51. Management's indication of narrower trading spreads at the beginning of the fourth quarter added uncertainty to the near-term revenue outlook. The shares declined 8.7% in pre-market trading as investors assessed these developments alongside the upcoming Federal Reserve decision.

REUTERS/David 'Dee' Delgado Oct 27 (Reuters) - Robinhood Markets missed Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit on Tuesday, as slower cryptocurrency trading and higher expenses overshadowed strong activity in options and prediction markets. Shares of the Menlo Park, California-based company fell 7% in after-hours trading. The trading platform's transaction-based revenue from cryptocurrencies fell 55% to $120 million from a year earlier. Crypto markets have come under pressure this year amid heightened volatility and persistent outflows, as inflationary pressures and higher interest rates make bonds and other traditional investments more attractive than speculative assets. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, has fallen as much as 8% year to date as geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices add to market uncertainty. Robinhood's overall transaction-based revenue rose about 19% to $867 million, driven by a more than sixfold increase in event-contracts revenue and a 31% jump in options revenue. However, revenue growth lagged the increase in trading contracts, suggesting that growth was becoming more concentrated in a few key areas, said Bill Birmingham, research head at REX Financial. "Prediction markets are becoming a second outlet for the same core active traders rather than a funnel for new customers," Birmingham said, adding that some of the volume may reflect a shift from existing trading activity rather than incremental business. Robinhood CFO Shiv Verma, however, emphasized that prediction markets was an important growth driver for the company. "Prediction markets is almost a $500-million-a-year business already, and so growing incredibly nicely, and it's less than two years old because it came out at the start of the 2024 election," Verma told journalists over a call. He said both sports and non-sports event contracts were growing strongly, with non-sports contracts accounting for a larger share of overall trading volume. The company's operating expenses rose 16% to $739 million for the three months ended September 30, driven by higher credit-loss provisions, spending on new businesses such as Trump Accounts and Rothera, and increased marketing. Robinhood posted a profit of 51 cents per share, missing analysts' expectations of a per-share profit of 55 cents, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. Robinhood reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.60, exceeding the consensus estimate of $0.55. However, revenue of approximately $1.42 billion fell short of market expectations, while reported earnings under generally accepted accounting principles declined year over year. Robinhood's third-quarter results showed a difference between adjusted profitability and its reported financial performance. GAAP diluted earnings per share declined 16% from the corresponding quarter of 2025 to $0.51, also falling short of expectations. The results indicated continued annual revenue growth, although the company faced weaker performance in certain trading activities and higher operating costs. Investors focused on these pressures despite the adjusted earnings beat, contributing to the decline in the company's share price before the market opened. The cryptocurrency business was a significant source of weakness during the third quarter. Robinhood reported cryptocurrency transaction revenue of $120 million, representing a decline of 55% compared with the same period last year. Cryptocurrency trading volume decreased 38% year over year, reducing the revenue generated from digital asset transactions. The decline affected the company's overall financial performance, even as other trading categories recorded growth. Revenue from equities, options and event contracts increased during the period, providing some offset to the weaker cryptocurrency business. The figures demonstrate the continued influence of cryptocurrency trading activity on Robinhood's financial results. Comments from Robinhood's management during the earnings conference call added to concerns about the company's near-term revenue outlook. Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma indicated that trading spreads had narrowed at the beginning of the fourth quarter. The observation raised questions about the revenue Robinhood may generate from transaction activity during the final months of 2026. Narrower spreads can affect the amount of revenue earned from certain trading transactions, potentially reducing the company's effective take rate. The comments therefore added uncertainty to the outlook for transaction-based revenue following the third-quarter decline in cryptocurrency activity. Investors will monitor whether the tighter spreads persist and how they affect the company's financial performance during the fourth quarter. Robinhood also reported an increase in operating expenses that exceeded its rate of revenue growth. Operating costs rose 16% year over year, compared with a 12% increase in total revenue. REUTERS/David 'Dee' Delgado Oct 27 (Reuters) - Robinhood Markets missed Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit on Tuesday, as slower cryptocurrency trading and higher expenses overshadowed strong activity in options and prediction markets. Shares of the Menlo Park, California-based company fell 7% in after-hours trading. The trading platform's transaction-based revenue from cryptocurrencies fell 55% to $120 million from a year earlier. Crypto markets have come under pressure this year amid heightened volatility and persistent outflows, as inflationary pressures and higher interest rates make bonds and other traditional investments more attractive than speculative assets. Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, has fallen as much as 8% year to date as geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices add to market uncertainty. Robinhood's overall transaction-based revenue rose about 19% to $867 million, driven by a more than sixfold increase in event-contracts revenue and a 31% jump in options revenue. However, revenue growth lagged the increase in trading contracts, suggesting that growth was becoming more concentrated in a few key areas, said Bill Birmingham, research head at REX Financial. "Prediction markets are becoming a second outlet for the same core active traders rather than a funnel for new customers," Birmingham said, adding that some of the volume may reflect a shift from existing trading activity rather than incremental business. Robinhood CFO Shiv Verma, however, emphasized that prediction markets was an important growth driver for the company. "Prediction markets is almost a $500-million-a-year business already, and so growing incredibly nicely, and it's less than two years old because it came out at the start of the 2024 election," Verma told journalists over a call. He said both sports and non-sports event contracts were growing strongly, with non-sports contracts accounting for a larger share of overall trading volume. The company's operating expenses rose 16% to $739 million for the three months ended September 30, driven by higher credit-loss provisions, spending on new businesses such as Trump Accounts and Rothera, and increased marketing. Robinhood posted a profit of 51 cents per share, missing analysts' expectations of a per-share profit of 55 cents, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. (Reporting by Prakhar Srivastava and Rishab Shaju in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara)

extraction.body: Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform. Introduced in Gemini and Google Search earlier this year, connected apps let users securely link and interact with popular third-party services, then use them to take specific actions. For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist. We’ve seen varying takes on the idea by other consumer-facing AI services like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse. The premise is that such integrations could ultimately shift consumer behavior away from launching and using individual apps to instead using their favorite services through their preferred AI provider. However, to successfully capture and retain consumers’ attention, there have to actually be a wide range of connected apps to explore. Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance. The platform preview is currently available in beta to developers in the U.S., and will allow developers to build and submit apps that can be used across Google’s products. To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains. Essentially, this process lets devs connect their app to Google’s services so it can be used with the search giant’s AI features. Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both. After the app is live, developers can track traffic, latency and error rates, and maintain control over their brand identity, such as their verified logos and authenticated accounts. Similar to how SEO allowed companies and websites show up search engine rankings, this could well be one of the initial steps for businesses that want their services to be more visible to users on the agentic web. Google already has over 50 Connected Apps available in Gemini, including from partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, Peloton, and others, in addition to its own expansive set of services, from Workplace and Photos to YouTube Music and Google Home. These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks. Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others. Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search. The new Connected Apps platform is in public preview for U.S. developers who sign up for the waitlist. Google did not share when it would become more broadly available. relevantPassages.text: Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search.
Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance.
Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform.
For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist.
Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both.
These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks.
Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others.
Google did not share when it would become more broadly available.

To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains.

extraction.body: Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform. Introduced in Gemini and Google Search earlier this year, connected apps let users securely link and interact with popular third-party services, then use them to take specific actions. For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist. We’ve seen varying takes on the idea by other consumer-facing AI services like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse. The premise is that such integrations could ultimately shift consumer behavior away from launching and using individual apps to instead using their favorite services through their preferred AI provider. However, to successfully capture and retain consumers’ attention, there have to actually be a wide range of connected apps to explore. Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance. The platform preview is currently available in beta to developers in the U.S., and will allow developers to build and submit apps that can be used across Google’s products. To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains. Essentially, this process lets devs connect their app to Google’s services so it can be used with the search giant’s AI features. Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both. After the app is live, developers can track traffic, latency and error rates, and maintain control over their brand identity, such as their verified logos and authenticated accounts. Similar to how SEO allowed companies and websites show up search engine rankings, this could well be one of the initial steps for businesses that want their services to be more visible to users on the agentic web. Google already has over 50 Connected Apps available in Gemini, including from partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, Peloton, and others, in addition to its own expansive set of services, from Workplace and Photos to YouTube Music and Google Home. These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks. Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others. Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search. The new Connected Apps platform is in public preview for U.S. developers who sign up for the waitlist. Google did not share when it would become more broadly available.
